title: Miso Soup
subtitle: simple Japanese dashi broth with miso and tofu
excerpt: Miso soup is a staple of Japanese meals. Dashi stock is gently warmed and miso paste is whisked in off the heat to preserve its fermented depth. With tofu, mushrooms, and spring onion, it is ready in 10 minutes.
sourceNotes: Miso soup has been a staple of the Japanese diet since at least the Kamakura period (1185--1333). It is made from dashi stock and miso paste dissolved into it. In Japan, it is served at almost every meal, including breakfast.

content.text: The key rule with miso soup is never to boil the miso. Boiling kills the fermented flavour. The stock is heated, the other ingredients go in, and only then is the miso whisked in off the heat. The whole thing takes 10 minutes.

items.prepNote: use dashi stock -- or make with dashi powder and water
use 3--4 tbsp white miso paste -- whisk into the hot stock off the heat
use 150g soft tofu -- cut into small cubes

content.text: Bring the dashi stock to a gentle simmer in a saucepan. Do not let it boil hard.
Add the rehydrated mushrooms if using. Simmer for 3 minutes.
Add the tofu cubes. Warm through for 1 minute.
Remove the pan from the heat. Whisk the miso paste into a ladleful of hot stock until smooth, then stir it back into the pan. Never boil miso -- it kills the flavour.
Ladle into bowls. Top with spring onion. Serve immediately.

items.cause: Miso added too early and boiled
items.fix: Always add miso off the heat. Boiling destroys the fermented flavour. If it has boiled, stir in a little more fresh miso paste before serving.

content.text: Miso soup is served at almost every Japanese meal. It is simple but the quality of the dashi and miso matters. White miso (shiro) is mild and sweet. Red miso (aka) is deeper and saltier. Most home cooks use a mix. The soup takes 10 minutes start to finish.
